{{Short description|Formula in matrix theory}}
{{No footnotes|date=January 2025}}

In [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix theory]], the '''Hadamard variation formula''' is a set of differential equations for how the eigenvalues of a time-varying Hermitian matrix with distinct eigenvalues change with time.

== Statement ==

Consider the space of <math display="inline">n\times n</math> Hermitian matrices with all eigenvalues distinct.

Let <math display="inline">A=A(t)</math> be a path in the space. Let <math display="inline">u_i, \lambda_i</math> be its eigenpairs.

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = If <math display="inline">A(t)</math> is first-differentiable, then <math display="inline">\dot{\lambda}_i=u_i^* \dot{A} u_i</math>

If <math display="inline">A(t)</math> is second-differentiable, then <math display="inline">\ddot \lambda_i=u_i^* \ddot{A} u_i+2 \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{\left|u_i^* \dot{A} u_j\right|^2}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}</math>
| name = Hadamard variation formula
| note = {{harvnb|Tao|2012|pages=48–49}}
}}

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}
Since <math display="inline">u_i^*u_i = 1</math> does not change with time, taking the derivative, we find that <math display="inline">\langle \dot u_i, u_i\rangle</math> is purely imaginary. Now, this is due to a unitary ambiguity in the choice of <math display="inline">u_i(t)</math>. Namely, for any first-differentiable <math display="inline">\theta(t)</math>, we can pick <math display="inline">v_i(t) := e^{i\theta(t)}u_i(t)</math> instead. In that case, we have <math display="block">
      \langle \dot v_i, v_i\rangle = \langle \dot u_i, u_i\rangle - i\dot\theta
      </math> so picking <math display="inline">\theta</math> such that <math display="inline">\dot\theta = -i\langle \dot u_i, u_i\rangle</math>, we have <math display="inline">\langle \dot v_i, v_i\rangle = 0</math>. Thus, WLOG, we assume that <math display="inline">\langle \dot u_i, u_i\rangle = 0</math>.

Take derivative of <math display="inline">Au_i = \lambda_i u_i</math>, <math display="block">
      \dot{A} u_i+A \dot{u}_i=\dot{\lambda}_i u_i+\lambda_i \dot{u}_i
      </math> Now take inner product with <math display="inline">u_i</math>.

Taking derivative of <math display="inline">\langle \dot u_i, u_i\rangle = 0</math>, we get <math display="block">
      \langle \ddot u_i, u_i\rangle = \langle u_i, \ddot u_i\rangle = -\langle \dot u_i, \dot u_i\rangle
      </math> and all terms are real.

Take derivative of <math display="inline">\dot{A} u_i+A \dot{u}_i=\dot{\lambda}_i u_i+\lambda_i \dot{u}_i</math>, then multiply by <math display="inline">u_i^*</math>, and simplify by <math display="inline">u_i^* \dot{u}_i=0</math>, <math display="inline">u_i^* A=\lambda_i u_i^*</math>, we get <math display="block">
      u_i^* \ddot{A} u_i+2 u_i^* \dot{A} \dot{u}_i=\ddot{\lambda}_i
      </math> - Expand <math display="inline">\dot{u}_i</math> in the eigenbasis <math display="inline">\left\{u_j\right\}</math> as <math display="inline">\dot{u}_i=\sum_{j \neq i} c_{i j} u_j</math>. Take derivative of <math display="inline">Au_i = \lambda_i u_i</math>, and multiply by <math display="inline">u_j^*A</math>, we obtain <math display="inline">c_{ij}=-\frac{u_j^* \dot{A} u_i}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}</math>.
{{hidden end}}Higher order generalizations appeared in {{Harvard citation|Tao|Vu|2011}}.
